Series::CalcAccessor::hess¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

template<class Fn>
Series Series::CalcAccessor::hess(Fn&& fn) const

What It Computes¶

hess() computes all second partial derivatives of a scalar-valued callback. For receiver shape X, the result shape is X + X. The first input-axis block identifies the gradient component being differentiated; the second identifies the variable used for that derivative.

For a vector receiver, this is the usual square Hessian matrix. For a matrix receiver of shape [r,c], the result has shape [r,c,r,c]; axes are not silently flattened. This makes contractions and axis-aware analysis explicit.

hess(fn) is the scalar-constrained equivalent of diff(fn, 2). It runs higher-order reverse mode, not finite differencing of a previously rounded gradient. The callback path therefore needs reverse rules that remain differentiable through second order.

Reading The Result¶

For vector x, entry [i,j] is

partial^2 fn(x) / (partial x[i] partial x[j])

Diagonal entries measure curvature along one variable. Off-diagonal entries measure coupling: they are zero for a sum of lane-local terms and nonzero when variables interact. Numerically equal cross-partials are expected for a smooth function, but hess() does not post-process or symmetrize the computed tensor.

Examples¶

Example 1. A sum of cubes has diagonal curvature 6x and no cross coupling.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto hessian = x.calc.hess(
    [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.pow(3.0).sum(); });

std::cout << hessian << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[12, 0],
  [0, 18]]

Example 2. Mixed terms appear off the diagonal. At (a,b)=(2,3), fn(a,b)=a^2*b+b^3 has cross-partials 2a=4.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto hessian = x.calc.hess([](const pluss::Series& z) {
  auto a = z.select(0, 0);
  auto b = z.select(0, 1);
  return a.square().mul(b).add(b.pow(3.0));
});

std::cout << hessian << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[6, 4],
  [4, 18]]

Example 3. A scalar receiver produces a rank-zero Hessian because each copy of an empty input shape contributes no axis.

auto x = pluss::make_series(0.5);
auto curvature = x.calc.hess(
    [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.sin(); });

std::cout << std::setprecision(10);
std::cout << curvature.item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

-0.4794255386

Example 4. hess() requires an actual scalar callback result. It never sums a vector implicitly because doing so would change the requested function.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
try {
  (void)x.calc.hess(
      [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.square(); });
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::string message = error.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

Series.calc.hess: function must return a rank-zero scalar Series

Cost And Storage¶

For N input lanes, the Hessian contains N^2 values. Keeping higher-rank axes does not change that count; it only preserves their meaning. Avoid materializing the full Hessian when an algorithm needs only a directional curvature or matrix-vector product. hess() is appropriate when every entry is actually consumed or when N is modest.

Options And Failure Modes¶

strict_dependency is honored. order and elementwise do not change the fixed scalar, second-order contract. Failures include an undefined callback result, a non-scalar result, a disconnected strict path, or an operation whose reverse rule does not support differentiation through the second pass.
